prize_parts.citation: For the invention and realisation of optical lattice clocks, enabling measurement of time at the 10^-18 level

statement.case_for: Optical lattice clocks are a single, well-bounded invention with a clear mechanism: Katori's magic-wavelength trapping cancels the lattice light shift while Lamb-Dicke confinement lets very many neutral atoms be interrogated on an ultranarrow transition, and Ye's group then drove the accuracy and stability to roughly 1e-18. The achievement is confirmed by many independent laboratories and species, validated by international clock comparisons, and already used for tests of fundamental constants, relativistic geodesy and the preparation of a new definition of the second. Three of eight members placed it first and six placed it in the top three, so it is the candidate on which the committee's scientific judgments overlap most. The credit is also the cleanest on the list: two people, one proposal-plus-realisation pairing, and the neighbouring recognitions (Hall and Hansch 2005 for the comb, Wineland 2012 for ion control) are adjacent rather than overlapping. From my own field I can judge that the control of systematic shifts, including blackbody, higher-order light shifts and collisional effects, is a substantial atomic-structure achievement and not only an engineering one.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is that the redefinition of the second has not yet happened, so part of the case rests on a pending application rather than a completed one, and some colleagues may see precision metrology as an instrument advance more than a discovery. There is also a genuine boundary question with ion clocks and with other lattice-clock groups at NIST, PTB, SYRTE and elsewhere who reached comparable performance, so two names are clean but not the only defensible allocation. I also rely on recollection for the exact priority history of the magic-wavelength idea, which the file does not settle, and a prize in a field I know closely risks my overrating how decisive the systematic-shift control is.

responses.point: Ulf ranks the Higgs discovery first as a clear, concrete and consequential experimental result, and accepts that any prize must choose among thousands of collaborators by leadership judgment.
responses.response: I agree that the Higgs observation is a first-rate scientific result and I do not dismiss it on merit; I ranked B039 low only because it was not on my list at all, not because of any judgment about its importance. My disagreement is about whether it can be awarded fairly. Ulf himself says the choice among Gianotti, Jenni, Virdee and Della Negra is a leadership judgment, and with a three-person cap that drops a founder of equal standing. The lattice-clock prize has no such problem: both people are the decisive originators. I would keep B039 as a serious option, but I do not think its credit problem is easier to resolve now than in earlier years.

responses.point: Stefan ranks lattice clocks first from a laser-spectroscopy standpoint, as a clear instrument advance with strong multi-lab confirmation and cleanly bounded credit, and ranks the ion-trap quantum-information entry second.
responses.response: I agree with the core of this and it matches my own reading of the maturity evidence. I would qualify his claim that the credit is cleanly bounded: the ion-clock community and groups at NIST, PTB and SYRTE built much of the maturity of the field, so the boundary is clean for the invention but not for the whole subject. On his second choice I partly differ. Cirac and Zoller are decisive for the 1995 gate proposal, but Wineland's 2012 prize and Haroche's work already cover control of single quantum systems, so B010 needs a sharper citation than B012 does before I would put it alongside it.

responses.point: Goran ranks circuit QED first, arguing that coupling a superconducting qubit to a resonator gave the leading solid-state route to quantum processors, while openly noting his own proximity to the field and that the 2025 prize already honoured superconducting circuits.
responses.response: I take his scientific case seriously and respect the disclosure of proximity. My reservation is the one he raises himself: the 2025 prize recognised macroscopic quantum tunnelling in superconducting circuits, so a second award in the same family so soon would need a clearly distinct discovery, and I am not yet convinced that circuit QED is read as distinct rather than as a follow-on. I would want that tested explicitly. Compared with lattice clocks, circuit QED also has a harder question of how much credit belongs to Yale, Delft, ETH and other contributors to the early circuit work.

responses.point: Bernhard ranks lattice clocks first, calling the credit compact and the field stable for over a decade, while noting that the boundary with earlier ion-clock and comb recognition needs care, and ranks topological insulators second.
responses.response: I agree that the boundary needs care and I think the 2005 and 2012 prizes are the right reference points: they honour the comb and ion control, not the neutral-atom lattice scheme. On his second choice I disagree in part. The Kane-Mele-Molenkamp trio is scientifically strong, but he and several others note that Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang proposed the HgTe realisation and Fu with Kane the three-dimensional case, none of whom could be added within the cap. That makes B057 more fragile on attribution than B012, whatever its conceptual depth.

responses.point: Eva Olsson ranks aberration-corrected electron optics first as a clear invention with lasting impact that is arguably overdue, and ranks twisted bilayer graphene second.
responses.response: I accept that aberration correction is mature and that Rose, Haider and Urban form a compact trio, and I do not see a scientific flaw in the case. Where I differ is on how it compares in discovery content: the achievement is a transformative instrument whose benefit is largely realised in other fields, whereas a lattice clock opens new fundamental measurement. That is a judgment about weighting, not a claim that microscopy is lesser. On twisted bilayer graphene I share her concern that the superconductivity is not yet understood, which weakens maturity compared with clocks.

uncertainties: Whether the committee treats lattice clocks and ion clocks as one field needing joint recognition rather than a bounded invention.
How much weight to give the still-pending redefinition of the second when judging maturity.
Exact priority details of the magic-wavelength proposal, which I have not verified independently from the provided files.
Whether a collaboration-based discovery (Higgs, IceCube) can ever be credited fairly under the three-person cap, which affects how I rank B012 against B039 and B029.
statement.conflict_note: My profile documents a long-running collaboration with Anne L'Huillier and papers with the Lund attosecond group and Ursula Keller's group at ETH Zurich, plus work with Reinhold Schuch, Marcus Dahlstrom, Luca Argenti and Paul Indelicato; none of these people are credited on any shortlisted entry, and nothing in the provided profile ties me to Katori or Ye. My field is close to precision atomic physics, so I would flag that proximity, but no specific conflict requiring recusal is apparent from the provided profile.
